ch5_ex9_q1: Isosceles triangles hide two identical right-angled triangles. Drop the line from the apex to the midpoint and the 10.6 m span becomes two 5.3 m bases.
ch5_ex9_q2: The mast (7.7 m) is almost twice the 4 m base distance, so $\tan\theta \approx 2$. That puts the angle a bit above $60^\circ$ ($\tan 60^\circ \approx 1.73$).
ch5_ex9_q3a: Estimate: $\tan 20^\circ \approx 0.36$, so the height is about $0.36 \times 5 = 1.8$ m.
ch5_ex9_q3b: Each strut joins the right angle to the midpoint of a rafter, which is the hypotenuse. The midpoint of a hypotenuse is the same distance from all three corners, so each strut is exactly half a rafter.
ch5_ex9_q4: Moving the foot away makes the ladder lean more, so the angle with the wall must increase from $20^\circ$. The answer $31^\circ 49'$ passes that check.
The ladder length stays 2.7 m: it is the hypotenuse both before and after the move.
ch5_ex9_q5: Estimate: $\tan 38^\circ \approx 0.78$, so $AB \approx 5 \div 0.78 \approx 6.4$ m and half of it is about 3.2. Then $\sqrt{5^2 + 3.2^2} \approx 5.9$.
ch5_ex9_q6: South and east are at right angles, so the two ground distances are the legs of a flat right triangle. Find both with $\dfrac{20}{\tan\theta}$, then use Pythagoras.
The smaller elevation angle ($27^\circ$) means Ginger is further away than Atlanta.
ch5_ex9_q7: The vertical leg is the height difference, $350 - 155 = 195$ cm. The angle is measured from the vertical wall, so the horizontal distance is opposite it: $195\tan 55^\circ$.
Common trap: the $55^\circ$ is not an angle of elevation. Check which line the angle touches before choosing tan or its reciprocal.
ch5_ex9_q8: Exact value: $\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$, so the height is $\dfrac{500}{\sqrt{3}} \approx 288.68$ m.
To hit a 40 m-high target from 500 m, the angle needed is only $\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{40}{500}\right) \approx 4.6^\circ$.
ch5_ex9_q9: Using complements avoids dividing: $\dfrac{1}{\tan 41^\circ} = \tan 49^\circ$, so the distance is $220(\tan 49^\circ - \tan 15^\circ)$.
ch5_ex9_q10: Distance sailed $= 893(\tan 76^\circ - \tan 63^\circ) \approx 1829$ m, using the angles measured at the peak ($90^\circ - 14^\circ$ and $90^\circ - 27^\circ$).
ch5_ex9_q11a: $\dfrac{10}{50} = 0.2$, and for small angles $\sin\theta \approx \theta$ in radians. $0.2$ rad $\approx 11.5^\circ$, matching $11^\circ 32'$.
ch5_ex9_q11b: BE is the diagonal across the desk top: $\sqrt{1.2^2 + 0.5^2} = 1.3$ m exactly. This is a scaled 5-12-13 triangle, so no calculator is needed.
Same 10 cm rise over a longer slope (1.3 m instead of 0.5 m) gives a gentler angle, so expect much less than $11^\circ$.
ch5_ex9_q12a: Every square's diagonal is side $\times \sqrt{2}$ (about 1.414 times the side). This is quicker than writing out Pythagoras.
ch5_ex9_q12b: $BG = \sqrt{25^2 + 45^2} = \sqrt{2650} = 5\sqrt{106}$. Factoring out 5 first ($5\sqrt{5^2 + 9^2}$) keeps the numbers small.
ch5_ex9_q12c: Symmetry shortcut: because the end is square, the bottom face and the side face are identical $25 \times 45$ rectangles, so their diagonals are equal.
ch5_ex9_q12d: Space-diagonal formula: $\sqrt{l^2 + w^2 + h^2} = \sqrt{45^2 + 25^2 + 25^2} = \sqrt{3275}$. It is Pythagoras used twice in one step.
ch5_ex9_q12e: The ratio $\dfrac{25}{45} = \dfrac{5}{9}$ is under 1, so the angle is under $45^\circ$.
ch5_ex9_q12f: The angle between a line and a plane is measured to the line's shadow on the plane. Here BE is the shadow of BH on the base, so the right angle is at E.
ch5_ex9_q12g: The diagonals of a rectangle bisect each other, so $OF = \tfrac{1}{2}BE \approx 25.74$. No new Pythagoras is needed.
ch5_ex9_q12h: FG is just a vertical edge of the cuboid, the same as the 25 cm height, so its midpoint splits it into 12.5 cm halves.
ch5_ex9_q12i: Both legs of triangle OFX are half those of triangle BEH ($OF = \tfrac{1}{2}BE$, $FX = \tfrac{1}{2}EH$), so the two triangles are similar. Scaling a triangle never changes its angles, so $\angle FOX = \angle EBH$.
ch5_ex9_q12j: Because triangle OFX is a half-scale copy of triangle BEH, $OX = \tfrac{1}{2}BH$. Check: $\sqrt{25.74^2 + 12.5^2} \approx 28.61$.
ch5_ex9_q13a: The angle a face makes with the base sits in the triangle with height 26 and half-side 6. Draw that triangle on its own before calculating.
A tall, thin pyramid (height more than four times the half-side) must have steep faces, so a large angle like $77^\circ$ makes sense.
ch5_ex9_q13b: Half-diagonal $= 6\sqrt{2} \approx 8.49$. It is longer than the half-side 6, so the edge angle is less steep than the face angle.
ch5_ex9_q13c: Exact working: edge $= \sqrt{26^2 + (6\sqrt{2})^2} = \sqrt{676 + 72} = \sqrt{748}$. No rounded angles are needed.
ch5_ex9_q14a: The adjacent side is half the base, $2.85$ cm. A common error is to use the full 5.7 cm.
ch5_ex9_q14b: General link for square pyramids: $\tan(\text{edge angle}) = \dfrac{\tan(\text{face angle})}{\sqrt{2}}$, because the half-diagonal is $\sqrt{2}$ times the half-side. Here $\dfrac{\tan 68^\circ}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 1.75$.
ch5_ex9_q15a: Use the complement to avoid dividing: half-side $= 47\tan 17^\circ$, so side $= 94\tan 17^\circ \approx 28.74$ cm.
ch5_ex9_q15b: Diagonal $= \text{side} \times \sqrt{2}$. Multiply the stored unrounded side by 1.414..., using the $\sqrt{\ }$ key.
ch5_ex9_q15c: Shortcut from the face angle: $\tan(\text{edge angle}) = \dfrac{\tan 73^\circ}{\sqrt{2}}$, giving $66^\circ 37'$ without needing the side length at all.
ch5_ex9_q16: Sine values creep up to 1 as the angle approaches $90^\circ$ but never reach it for an acute angle: $\sin 89^\circ \approx 0.9998$.
Link: cosine of an acute angle is also between 0 and 1, but tangent can be any positive number.
ch5_ex9_q17a: Only the depth (7.4) and height (4.8) matter. The 10 cm length runs along the blade's edge, so it never appears in the triangle.
Angles on a straight line: the blade is $\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{7.4}{4.8}\right) \approx 57.03^\circ$ from the downward vertical, so $180^\circ - 57.03^\circ$ from the upward vertical.
ch5_ex9_q17b: Halving the horizontal distance makes the blade closer to vertical, so the angle from the downward vertical drops (from $57^\circ$ to about $38^\circ$).
ch5_ex9_q18a: Scale factor: 1 cm : 20 m means multiply plan lengths by 20 to get metres, so $4.5 \times 20 = 90$ m.
ch5_ex9_q18b: Easier-to-remember form: $h = \dfrac{d}{\dfrac{1}{\tan\theta_1} + \dfrac{1}{\tan\theta_2}}$, because the two base pieces are $\dfrac{h}{\tan\theta_1}$ and $\dfrac{h}{\tan\theta_2}$.
ch5_ex9_q18c: Both angles are steep ($72^\circ$ and $88^\circ$), so the tree is much further away than the baseline is long. 250 m against a 90 m baseline is reasonable.
ch5_ex9_q19a: $140^\circ$T is $50^\circ$ past east, or equivalently S$40^\circ$E. Writing it as a compass bearing tells you which acute angle to mark.
ch5_ex9_q19b: Shortcut: north $= 7 + 13\cos 140^\circ \approx -2.96$. The negative result means south.
ch5_ex9_q19c: East $= 13\sin 140^\circ \approx 8.36$ km and south $\approx 2.96$ km. Bearing $= 90^\circ + \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2.96}{8.36}\right) \approx 109.5^\circ$, right on the rounding boundary.
ch5_ex9_q20: Set up axes along the direct line: the ball is $315\cos 10^\circ \approx 310.2$ m along it and $315\sin 10^\circ \approx 54.7$ m off to the side.
Remaining distance along the line is $630 - 310.2 \approx 319.8$ m. The ball is still about halfway, so 324.4 m to go is sensible.
ch5_ex9_q21a: A radius meets a tangent at $90^\circ$, which creates the right-angled triangle tip-contact-centre. That is the key fact for any ball-in-cone problem.
ch5_ex9_q21b: Tip to centre $= \dfrac{2.5}{\sin 18^\circ} \approx 8.09$. The bottom of the ball is one radius lower, at $8.09 - 2.5 \approx 5.59$ above the tip, so $h = 12.5 - 5.59$.
Fun exact value: $\sin 18^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt{5} - 1}{4}$, so tip to centre $= 2.5(\sqrt{5} + 1)$ exactly.
